script.opening: “Hello, it’s Siobhan O’Connor, Bridget O’Connor’s daughter. I got the letter about Mum’s bloods — it says you want to refer her urgently to the hospital for her bowel. I’ve got power of attorney for her health. Mum would hate that. Can I just say no?”

facts.text: If asked: gives Mum’s date of birth (14 March 1943) and address. “It’s a health and welfare one. Registered in 2021. I’m the only attorney. I think there was a box about life-sustaining treatment — I ticked that I could decide.” Has the access code from the Office of the Public Guardian “somewhere in my emails” if asked.

“She knows me most days but not always. She can’t follow a conversation for long. She doesn’t know what year it is.” Needs help with washing, dressing and meals; walks round the house; eats well “when I sit with her”. Sleeps a lot.

If asked: “She’s paler and more tired. No pain that I can tell.” Bowels: “Her pads are sometimes a bit darker. I haven’t seen red blood.” Not losing weight “that I’ve noticed”. No vomiting. No breathlessness or falls.

If asked what Mum was like and what she valued: “A school cook for thirty years. Very Catholic. When Dad was dying in hospital in 2015 she said, ‘Don’t ever let them do that to me — tubes and cameras. Let me die at home with my rosary.’ She said it more than once.” No written advance decision.
“Last year she was in A&E with a urine infection for nine hours. She screamed, pulled out her drip, didn’t eat. It took her weeks to settle.”
Brother, 49, lives in Málaga, phones weekly. “He says if there’s cancer they should find it and fix it and I’m giving up on her. He hasn’t seen her since Christmas. He doesn’t see what it’s like.”

Carers twice a day (morning and evening). Siobhan works part-time as a medical receptionist at another practice and visits every day. If asked about herself: “I’m exhausted. I haven’t had a day off in a year.”

Only if asked how she is coping, or what else is on her mind: “If I’m honest, I’ve been looking at care homes. And I feel terrible. Declan will say I’m saying no to the test because it’s easier for me.” Quietly tearful.

Articulate, organised, defensive at first. Start with “Can I just say no?” If the doctor simply says “yes, you’re the attorney, it’s your call” — accept, but sound uneasy. If the doctor says “you can’t refuse, we must refer” — become angry: “Then what’s the point of the LPA?” If the doctor explains the LPA properly, talks about what Mum would have wanted, and offers a joint discussion including Declan, soften and engage. Reveal exhaustion and care-home thoughts only if asked about yourself.

ice.ideas: “The LPA means I decide, and Mum wouldn’t want hospital tests.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is exhausted, has been looking at care homes, feels guilty, and fears her brother will accuse her of choosing what is easier for her rather than what Mum would want. She says this only if asked how she is coping.
ice.expectations: To be told she can refuse the referral; underneath, help to make a decision she can defend to her brother and live with.

cues: “Can I just say no?” — wants confirmation of her authority; needs it explained accurately.
“Let me die at home with my rosary” — clear past wishes and religious values, central to best interests.
“He doesn’t see what it’s like” — family conflict and carer strain.

data.kind: Blood results and FIT (taken 8 days ago)
values: 10 or more = suspected cancer pathway referral

checkpoints.text: Confirms the caller’s identity and checks the LPA: health and welfare (not property and finance), registered, sole attorney, scope including life-sustaining treatment, any conditions — using the copy on file or the Office of the Public Guardian access code

Explains the results honestly and in plain language (iron-deficiency anaemia with blood in the stool test — a possible bowel cancer that needs to be considered), and asks about symptoms (bleeding, weight loss, pain, breathlessness, falls)
Explores Bridget’s current function and her past wishes, beliefs and values (no hospitals, “die at home with my rosary”, Catholic faith, previous distress in hospital)

Explains accurately what the LPA allows: it applies only to decisions Bridget lacks capacity to make, assessed for this decision; the attorney must decide in her best interests (not their own preference); can consent to or refuse treatment offered; cannot demand treatment clinicians do not think appropriate

Sets out realistic options without bias — referral to discuss with the specialist team (tests adapted to her, possibly less invasive), or not investigating with iron treatment and symptom-led care — with benefits and burdens of each

Plans a capacity assessment for this decision, a best-interests discussion including Declan and the carers, starts oral iron now, documents, and explains that unresolved disagreement can go to the Court of Protection

Acknowledges the weight of the decision and the family conflict, asks how Siobhan is coping, and responds to her exhaustion and guilt (carer’s assessment, respite, care-home discussion without judgement)
Avoids both “you decide” and “you can’t refuse” — supports a shared, well-reasoned decision and agrees clear next steps and a follow-up date

worked.txt: “Before I discuss your mum, can I check a few details? … Thank you. We have a copy of your health and welfare LPA on her record — registered in 2021, and you’re the only attorney. That helps.”

“Your mum’s blood count is low because she’s short of iron, and the stool test found blood. At her age, one of the possible causes is a bowel cancer — which is why the letter suggested a referral. It doesn’t mean it is cancer, but it’s a possibility we have to take seriously.”

“Your LPA lets you make health decisions for your mum when she can’t make that particular decision herself. You make it in her best interests — what she would have wanted and what’s best for her now, not what any of us would choose for ourselves. You can say yes or no to things we offer, but you can’t ask for something the doctors don’t think would help.”
“Tell me about your mum before the dementia — what mattered to her?” … “So she was clear: no tubes and cameras, home, her faith. That counts for a lot.”

“There are two reasonable paths. One is a referral just to talk with the specialist team — they might suggest a gentler test, or agree not to investigate. The other is not to investigate, treat the anaemia with iron, and look after her at home if symptoms come. Neither is giving up.”

“The law asks us to consult the people who care about her, including Declan, even though the decision is yours. How about a three-way call this week with me, you and Declan, and the carers’ views — so it’s a decision you can all understand?”

f.learning: A health and welfare LPA gives the attorney authority only when the donor lacks capacity for the specific decision, and only to decide in the donor’s best interests (MCA 2005 s4): her past and present wishes, beliefs and values, the views of people close to her, and the least restrictive option. The attorney can consent to or refuse treatment offered (refusing life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly allows it) but cannot insist on treatment. A positive FIT with iron deficiency in advanced dementia is a genuine best-interests decision: present realistic options, assess capacity for this decision, consult family and carers, treat the anaemia, support the carer, document — and if agreement cannot be reached, the Court of Protection decides.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: Mental Capacity Act 2005 (sections 1–4, 9–11) and Code of Practice (2007) · Office of the Public Guardian: lasting power of attorney guidance and “Use a lasting power of attorney” service · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated 2026) · NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) FIT to guide colorectal cancer pathway referral in primary care · NICE NG97 Dementia (2018) · GMC Decision making and consent (2020) · GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010, updated 2022)
knowledge.summary: FIT 85 with iron deficiency in an 83-year-old with advanced dementia; the daughter is her health and welfare attorney. Explain what the LPA allows, assess capacity for this decision, and reach a best-interests decision together.

points.t: Hb 92 with low MCV and ferritin 6 is iron-deficiency anaemia; FIT 85 µg Hb/g is well above the 10 threshold. NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer with FIT 10 or more. Coeliac serology is negative.

Overt rectal bleeding, a palpable mass, weight loss, obstruction symptoms (vomiting, distension, absolute constipation), breathlessness, chest pain or falls from anaemia — these change urgency and comfort needs.

A registered health and welfare LPA can be used only when the donor lacks capacity for the decision in question. The attorney stands in the donor’s shoes for that decision, must act in her best interests and follow the MCA principles. Refusal of life-sustaining treatment requires express authority in the LPA. Attorneys cannot demand treatment.

Assess whether Bridget can understand, retain, use or weigh the information about the referral and communicate a choice, with support. Advanced dementia makes incapacity likely but it must still be assessed and recorded for this decision.

Consider her past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values (Catholic faith, “no tubes and cameras”, distress in hospital), what she would have taken into account, and the views of family (Declan), carers and the attorney. Choose the least restrictive option.

Referral to discuss with the specialist team (who may offer CT colonography or a clinic-only discussion); or no investigation with oral iron, symptom-led care and advance care planning. Oral iron (for example ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily or on alternate days) is reasonable now in either path.

If the attorney’s decision does not appear to be in the person’s best interests, or the family cannot agree, seek a second opinion, a best-interests meeting, advice from the Office of the Public Guardian, or an application to the Court of Protection.
Heavy bleeding, collapse, vomiting with a swollen tummy, or breathlessness — same-day contact or 999 in keeping with her wishes; a ReSPECT conversation is worth planning.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee. Before we talk about your mum, could you confirm her date of birth and address? … Thank you. I can see we have your health and welfare LPA on her record. What would you like to get out of our call?
model.why: Confirms identity, checks the LPA, sets the agenda

model.text: The letter says urgent hospital referral for her bowel. Mum would hate it. I’ve got power of attorney — can I just say no?

That’s an important question and I’ll answer it properly. First, can I explain what the tests showed? Her blood count is low because she’s short of iron, and the stool test found blood. At her age a bowel cancer is one possible cause — it doesn’t mean it is one.
model.why: Honest, plain explanation of the results

model.text: I guessed that’s what it meant.
Have you noticed any bleeding, weight loss, tummy pain, or her getting more breathless or falling?
Pads a bit darker sometimes. No pain, no weight loss that I can see. Just pale and tired.
Tell me about your mum before the dementia — what mattered to her about her health?
model.why: Gathers past wishes, beliefs and values

model.text: She said after Dad died in hospital: no tubes and cameras, let me die at home with my rosary. And last year in A&E she was terrified.

That’s really important. So, about the LPA: it lets you decide when she can’t make that particular decision herself — and you decide in her best interests: what she would have wanted and what’s best for her now. You can say yes or no to what we offer, but not ask for something doctors don’t think would help. I’d also need to check her capacity for this decision — I can do that with you there.
model.why: Explains the LPA, best interests and capacity accurately

model.text: You could, if that’s in her best interests. There are two reasonable paths: a referral just to discuss with the specialist team — they may offer a gentler test or agree not to test — or not investigating, starting iron, and caring for her at home if symptoms come. The law also asks me to consult people close to her. How does Declan feel?
model.why: Balanced options and duty to consult

model.text: He says I’m giving up on her. He doesn’t see what it’s like.
That sounds hard. How are you doing yourself, with all of this?
Exhausted. I’ve been looking at care homes… and I feel terrible. He’ll say I’m choosing what’s easier for me.

Thank you for telling me. Looking after yourself isn’t selfish, and looking at care homes isn’t giving up. Let’s keep the two decisions separate: the test decision is about your mum’s wishes; your exhaustion deserves its own help — a carer’s assessment and respite. Would a three-way call with you and Declan this week help, so he hears her wishes and the options too?
model.why: Responds to guilt and separates carer needs from best interests

model.text: So: I’ll start iron tablets today, visit to assess her capacity for this decision with you there, and set up a call with Declan, including the carers’ views. We’ll record what we decide and why. If we really couldn’t agree, the Court of Protection can help — but I don’t think it will come to that. If she bleeds heavily, collapses or gets breathless, call us or 999. Does that plan feel right?
model.why: Concrete plan, documentation, dispute route and safety-net

model.text: Yes. That feels fairer — to Mum and to me.
I’ll also ask social care about a carer’s assessment. I’ll call you on Thursday to fix a time with Declan.

social.t: Daily caring for a parent with advanced dementia while working is exhausting; guilt about care homes is common. Offer a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014), respite and Carers UK / Dementia UK Admiral Nurses.
Family members who visit rarely may push for more intervention; a joint conversation centred on the person’s own wishes often resolves this.

legal.t: Presume capacity; support decision-making; unwise decisions are not incapacity; act in best interests; least restrictive option.

A registered health and welfare LPA operates only when the donor lacks capacity for the decision. Check registration, scope and any instructions; the OPG online service lets professionals view an LPA with an access code.
Decides disputes about best interests or an attorney’s conduct; the OPG investigates concerns about attorneys.

professional.t: An attorney acting under a valid health and welfare LPA is entitled to relevant information to make decisions within their authority. Confirm identity on the telephone.
Record the capacity assessment, the LPA check, the options discussed, who was consulted, the decision and the reasoning.

community.t: Dementia UK Admiral Nurse helpline, Alzheimer’s Society, Carers UK, local carers’ centre, parish support.

Breathlessness, chest pain, falls from anaemia

playbook.diagnosis: Iron-deficiency anaemia with FIT 85 µg Hb/g in an 83-year-old with advanced Alzheimer’s disease — colorectal cancer must be considered; whether to investigate is a best-interests decision for her attorney after a capacity assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your mum is short of iron and there’s blood in the stool test. A bowel cancer is one possible cause. The question now is what she would want us to do about that.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to protect your mum from something she always said she didn’t want — that matters, and the law asks us to give it weight.”
management.psychosocial: Separate the best-interests decision from carer exhaustion; offer a carer’s assessment and respite.
sharedPlan: Capacity assessment for the referral decision (home or video, with Siobhan present)
Best-interests discussion with Siobhan, Declan and carers this week
Decide: referral to discuss with specialists versus no investigation with symptom-led care; document
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, collapse, breathlessness — urgent contact or 999 in keeping with her wishes

pitfalls.intro: This station tests accurate knowledge of the MCA and LPAs under emotional pressure. It is failed by either handing the decision over with no best-interests process, or overruling the attorney.

items.fail: “You’re the attorney, so it’s entirely up to you.”
items.why: Ignores the capacity assessment and the duty to decide in best interests and consult others.
items.fix: Explain how an attorney decides and offer a structured discussion.

items.fail: “You can’t refuse — guidelines say we must refer.”
items.why: Wrong in law; NG12 informs, it does not compel. A valid attorney can refuse treatment offered.
items.fix: Present referral as an option weighed in best interests.

items.fail: Not checking the type, registration or scope of the LPA.
items.why: A property and finance LPA gives no authority over health decisions.
items.fix: Check the copy on file or the OPG access code.

items.fail: Not asking what Bridget would have wanted.
items.why: Past wishes and values are central to best interests.
items.fix: “Tell me about your mum before the dementia.”

items.fail: Missing the carer’s exhaustion and guilt.
items.why: Unspoken carer strain distorts the decision and the family dynamic.
items.fix: Ask how she is coping; offer a carer’s assessment.

items.why: Iron is low-burden and helps whatever is decided about investigation.

wordPics.clearFail: Tells her she cannot refuse, or that it is simply her call; no explanation of the results; no capacity or best-interests process; misses the carer strain.
wordPics.fail: Explains the results but gives an inaccurate account of the LPA, does not explore Bridget’s wishes, or leaves no concrete plan.
wordPics.pass: Checks the LPA, explains the results and what the attorney can do, explores past wishes, offers options and plans a capacity assessment and best-interests discussion.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: balances the options without bias, involves the brother constructively, starts iron, separates carer exhaustion from the decision and offers support, documents and names the Court of Protection route calmly.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: balances the options without bias, involves the brother constructively, starts iron, separates carer exhaustion from the decision and offers support, documents and names the Court of Protection route calmly.

avoid.dont: “It’s your decision as attorney — just let us know.”
avoid.instead: “You make the decision in her best interests — let’s work through what she would have wanted together.”
avoid.why: Attorneys need a best-interests process, not a blank cheque.

avoid.dont: “The guidelines say she must be referred.”
avoid.instead: “The guidelines say we should offer a referral. Whether it’s right for her is the decision we need to make.”
avoid.why: Guidelines inform; they do not override best interests.

avoid.dont: “Don’t feel guilty about the care home.”
avoid.instead: “Looking after yourself isn’t selfish. Let’s get you some help with that too.”
